entries: Begin here. It is raining. I look out on the maple, where a few leaves have turned yellow, and listen to Punch, the parrot, talking to himself and to the rain ticking gently against the windows.
May Sarton, Journal of a Solitude, the first entry, September 15th (W. W. Norton, 1973)
Diary
Beloved Pan, and all ye other gods who haunt this place, give me beauty in the inward soul; and may the outward and inward man be at one.
Plato, Phaedrus, 279b to 279c, the closing prayer (Socrates) (trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1892)
Philosophy

I don’t know exactly what a prayer is. / I do know how to pay attention, how to fall down / into the grass, how to kneel down in the grass, / how to be idle and blessed, how to stroll through the fields, / which is what I have been doing all day.
Mary Oliver, The Summer Day, lines 11 to 15, House of Light (Beacon Press, 1990)
Poetry
There was no possibility of taking a walk that day.
Charlotte Brontë, Jane Eyre, ch. 1, the opening sentence (Jane Eyre) (Smith, Elder and Co., 1847)
Fiction

Corrected: the speaker is now named after the locator. The title page presents the book as Jane Eyre: An Autobiography, edited by Currer Bell, and Jane narrates throughout in the first person, so the year’s practice of naming first person narrators applies here as it does to Jim Burden and Jake Barnes. The wording is unchanged.
We must reserve a back shop all our own, entirely free, in which to establish our real liberty and our principal retreat and solitude.
Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book I, ch. 39, Of Solitude (trans. Donald M. Frame, 1958)
Essay
But to look at the stars always makes me dream, as simply as I dream over the black dots of a map representing towns and villages.
Vincent van Gogh, The Complete Letters, letter 506 to Theo, Arles, c. 9 July 1888 (trans. Johanna van Gogh-Bonger, 1958)
Correspondence

I pray the gods to quit me of my toils, / To close the watch I keep, this livelong year; / For as a watch-dog lying, not at rest, / Propped on one arm, upon the palace-roof / Of Atreus’ race, too long, too well I know / The starry conclave of the midnight sky, / Too well, the splendours of the firmament, / The lords of light, whose kingly aspect shows— / What time they set or climb the sky in turn— / The year’s divisions, bringing frost or fire.
Aeschylus, Agamemnon, the opening speech, lines 1 to 10 (the Watchman) (trans. E. D. A. Morshead, 1881)
Drama

Corrected: Morshead does not print a full stop at line six. It ends in a comma and the sentence runs on, so the quotation now runs to line ten and closes on his own full stop. Line eight reads shows in the 1881 first edition and signs in the revised second edition of 1889.

In autumn the evenings, when the glittering sun sinks close to the edge of the hills and the crows fly back to their nests in threes and fours and twos; more charming still is a file of wild geese, like specks in the distant sky.
Sei Shōnagon, The Pillow Book, section 1, the autumn sentence of the opening list (trans. Ivan Morris, 1967)
Diary
I have discovered that all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.
Blaise Pascal, Pensées, section II, no. 139 in the Brunschvicg order (trans. W. F. Trotter, 1908)
Philosophy

And I shall have some peace there, for peace comes dropping slow, / Dropping from the veils of the morning to where the cricket sings; / There midnight’s all a glimmer, and noon a purple glow, / And evening full of the linnet’s wings.
W. B. Yeats, The Lake Isle of Innisfree, the second stanza, lines 5 to 8, The Rose (1893)
Poetry

When I pass the apple stalls I cannot help stopping and staring until I feel that I, myself, am changing into an apple, too—and that at any moment I may produce an apple, miraculously, out of my own being like the conjurer produces the egg.
Katherine Mansfield, Collected Letters, vol. 1, to Dorothy Brett, 11 October 1917 (ed. O’Sullivan and Scott, 1984)
Correspondence

What a strange, demented feeling it gives me when I realize I have spent whole days before this inkstone, with nothing better to do, jotting down at random whatever nonsensical thoughts have entered my head.
Yoshida Kenkō, Essays in Idleness (Tsurezuregusa), the Preface (trans. Donald Keene, 1967)
Essay
Above all, he learned from it how to listen, to listen with a still heart, with a waiting, open soul, without passion, without desire, without judgment, without opinions.
Hermann Hesse, Siddhartha, part two, The Ferryman (trans. Hilda Rosner, 1951)
Fiction
Some time now past in the Autumnal Tide, / When Phœbus wanted but one hour to bed, / The trees all richly clad, yet void of pride, / Where gilded o’re by his rich golden head.
Anne Bradstreet, Contemplations, stanza 1, lines 1 to 4, Several Poems, 1678 (ed. J. H. Ellis, 1867, p. 370)
Poetry

Corrected: the ligature in Phœbus stands, because the page prints it. Where in line four is not a slip. Ellis follows the 1678 sheets and reads Where gilded o’re, and modern editions emend it to Were. The long s in past is expanded. The 1678 sheets themselves were not opened.

They do come to you; but you do not hear them. You have not sat in the field in the evening listening for them. When the angelus rings you cross yourself and have done with it; but if you prayed from your heart, and listened to the thrilling of the bells in the air after they stop ringing, you would hear the voices as well as I do.
Bernard Shaw, Saint Joan, scene V, the ambulatory in the cathedral of Rheims (Joan)
Drama
There was no one waterfall above another—it was a sound of waters in the air—the voice of the air.
Dorothy Wordsworth, The Grasmere Journal, 29 April 1802, in Journals of Dorothy Wordsworth, ed. William Knight (Macmillan, 1897), p. 114
Diary
Leisure is a form of silence, of that silence which is the prerequisite of the apprehension of reality: only the silent hear and those who do not remain silent do not hear.
Josef Pieper, Leisure the Basis of Culture, the title essay, ch. III, pp. 40 to 41 (trans. Alexander Dru, 1952)
Philosophy

Corrected: the pages given are those of the Pantheon Books edition of 1952, not Faber, and the passage sits in chapter III of the title essay. The title in the Dru translation carries no comma. Gerald Malsbary renders the same sentence quite differently in 1998, so the translator must be named.
Evening, all things thou bringest / Which dawn spread apart from each other; / The lamb and the kid thou bringest, / Thou bringest the boy to his mother.
Sappho, fragment 95 in Wharton’s Sappho, the Hesperus fragment (trans. J. A. Symonds, 1883)
Poetry
Lying is done with words, and also with silence.
Adrienne Rich, On Lies, Secrets, and Silence, ‘Women and Honor: Some Notes on Lying’, 1975 (W. W. Norton, 1979)
Essay
You stir man to take pleasure in praising you, because you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.
Augustine of Hippo, Confessions, Book I, ch. 1 (I.i.1) (trans. Henry Chadwick, 1991)
Philosophy
What one seems to want in art, in experiencing it, is the same thing that is necessary for its creation, a self-forgetful, perfectly useless concentration.
Elizabeth Bishop, letter to Anne Stevenson, 8 January 1964, the Darwin letter, excerpted in Elizabeth Bishop and Her Art (1983)
Correspondence

Corrected the edition. The wording is confirmed, and the passage was first made public as an excerpt in Elizabeth Bishop and Her Art in 1983. The Library of America volume of 2008 prints letters to Anne Stevenson, but that this one is among them could not be confirmed, so it is not cited.
At any rate, that is happiness; to be dissolved into something complete and great.
Willa Cather, My Ántonia, Book I, The Shimerdas, ch. II (Jim Burden) (1918)
Fiction

Corrected the locator. The sentence is not the closing words of the chapter but the second to last. Book I, chapter II ends with the sentence beginning When it comes to one. Cather frames the whole narrative as Jim Burden’s manuscript, so the speaker stands.
Now we will count to twelve / and we will all keep still.
Pablo Neruda, Keeping Quiet, the opening two lines, Extravagaria (trans. Alastair Reid, 1972)
Poetry

Corrected the year. Alastair Reid’s Extravagaria was first published by Jonathan Cape in 1972, and Farrar, Straus and Giroux issued the American bilingual edition in 1974. The Spanish original is A callarse in Estravagario, Losada, 1958. The wording is attested in independent reprints crediting Reid. No printed copy was opened, so no page is given.
Noise is the most impertinent of all forms of interruption. It is not only an interruption, but also a disruption of thought.
Arthur Schopenhauer, Parerga and Paralipomena, ‘On Noise’, in Studies in Pessimism (trans. T. Bailey Saunders, 1890)
Essay
Why, yes, it is Sunday every day, in every house, when people open their eyes.
Maurice Maeterlinck, The Blue Bird, Act IV, scene 2 (the Happiness of Being Well) (trans. Alexander Teixeira de Mattos, 1909)
Drama
There is a really deep well inside me. And in it dwells God. Sometimes I am there, too.
Etty Hillesum, An Interrupted Life: The Diaries of Etty Hillesum 1941 to 1943, the entry of 26 August 1941 (trans. Arno Pomerans, 1983)
Diary

Corrected the translator credit. An Interrupted Life prints its translator as Arno Pomerans, not Arnold J. Pomerans, though the two names belong to the same man. No page is given because no copy of the edition was opened. For a diary the dated entry is the locator.
While washing the dishes one should only be washing the dishes, which means that while washing the dishes one should be completely aware of the fact that one is washing the dishes.
Thich Nhat Hanh, The Miracle of Mindfulness, ch. 1, ‘The Essential Discipline’, p. 3 (trans. Mobi Ho, 1976)
Philosophy

Corrected the locator. The sentence stands in chapter One, The Essential Discipline, on page 3, not in chapter Two. The earlier citation printed the section heading Washing the dishes to wash the dishes where the chapter title belongs. Beacon’s contents page puts chapter Two at page 11, well after this passage. The wording is verbatim.
Till rising and gliding out I wander’d off by myself, / In the mystical moist night-air, and from time to time, / Look’d up in perfect silence at the stars.
Walt Whitman, When I Heard the Learn’d Astronomer, the closing lines, Leaves of Grass, p. 214 (David McKay, 1891 to 1892)
Poetry

Corrected the edition. An earlier citation named a printing nobody had opened and it was dropped, leaving none. The 1891 to 1892 McKay printing has now been read: its own contents page puts the poem at page 214 in the By the Roadside cluster, and its text matches this card exactly.

Meanwhile, let us have a sip of tea. The afternoon glow is brightening the bamboos, the fountains are bubbling with delight, the soughing of the pines is heard in our kettle. Let us dream of evanescence, and linger in the beautiful foolishness of things.
Okakura Kakuzō, The Book of Tea, ch. I, The Cup of Humanity, the closing words (1906)
Essay

Corrected the punctuation. The 1906 text reads: let us dream of evanescence, and linger in the beautiful foolishness of things, with a comma before and. Okakura wrote the book in English, so no translator is named.
Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.
Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, proposition 7, the closing line (trans. C. K. Ogden, 1922)
Philosophy
Every landscape is, as it were, a state of the soul, and whoever penetrates into both is astonished to find how much likeness there is in each detail.
Henri-Frédéric Amiel, Amiel’s Journal, entry for 31 October 1852 (trans. Mrs Humphry Ward, 1885)
Diary

unused.quote: A very strange and solemn feeling came over me as I stood there, with no sound but the rustle of the pines, no one near me, and the sun so glorious, as for me alone.
unused.source: Louisa May Alcott, Her Life, Letters, and Journals, ch. III, Fruitlands, journal entry headed Concord, Thursday (ed. Cheney, 1889)

unused.quote: In the highlands you woke up in the morning and thought: Here I am, where I ought to be.
unused.source: Isak Dinesen, Out of Africa, Book One, Kamante and Lulu, ch. 1, The Ngong Farm (Putnam, 1937)
unused.note: Corrected the locator. Book One is titled Kamante and Lulu and The Ngong Farm is its first chapter, so the proposal gave the chapter title in the place of the book title. The wording is exact. Blixen wrote the book in English, so no translator is named.

unused.quote: Every one knows what attention is. It is the taking possession by the mind, in clear and vivid form, of one out of what seem several simultaneously possible objects or trains of thought.
unused.source: William James, The Principles of Psychology, vol. I, ch. XI, ‘Attention’, pp. 403 to 404 (Henry Holt, 1890)

unused.quote: For all the toll the desert takes of a man it gives compensations, deep breaths, deep sleep, and the communion of the stars.
unused.source: Mary Austin, The Land of Little Rain, ch. 1, ‘The Land of Little Rain’ (Houghton Mifflin, 1903)

unused.quote: Mysticism is the art of union with Reality.
unused.source: Evelyn Underhill, Practical Mysticism, ch. I, ‘What is Mysticism?’, the displayed definition (1914)

unused.quote: This being the case, if I were asked to name the chief benefit of the house, I should say: the house shelters daydreaming, the house protects the dreamer, the house allows one to dream in peace.
unused.source: Gaston Bachelard, The Poetics of Space, ch. 1, ‘The House. From Cellar to Garret’, p. 6 (trans. Maria Jolas, 1964)
unused.note: Corrected the wording against the Jolas scan at the Internet Archive. The sentence begins This being the case, and the edition spells daydreaming as one word: the hyphen that circulates online is an end of line break in the scan. The page, 6, is added.

unused.quote: Silence remains, inescapably, a form of speech (in many instances, of complaint or indictment) and an element in a dialogue.
unused.source: Susan Sontag, Styles of Radical Will, ‘The Aesthetics of Silence’, the opening essay (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1969)

unused.quote: Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, / O stranger worn with toil, / To a land of all lands the goodliest / Colonus’ glistening soil.
unused.source: Sophocles, Oedipus at Colonus, the Colonus ode, first strophe, from line 668 (the Chorus) (trans. F. Storr, 1912)

unused.quote: Thousands at his bidding speed / And post o’re Land and Ocean without rest: / They also serve who only stand and waite.
unused.source: John Milton, When I consider how my light is spent, lines 12 to 14, Poems (1673)
unused.note: Corrected the edition. The old spellings o’re and waite belong to the Poems of 1673, verified in the Milton Reading Room text of that edition. Beeching’s Oxford text of 1900 was not opened and is not claimed. The quotation begins inside line 12, which opens Is Kingly.

unused.quote: Up the dome of heaven / Like a great hill, / I watch them marching / Stately and still, / And I know that I / Am honored to be / Witness / Of so much majesty.
unused.source: Sara Teasdale, Stars, the last two stanzas, lines 13 to 20, Flame and Shadow, Part I (Macmillan, 1920)
unused.note: Corrected: the poem runs to twenty lines in five stanzas, so its closing two stanzas are lines 13 to 20 and not lines 17 to 24. The wording, capitals and punctuation are those of the 1920 text. The alternating indents of the printed page cannot be shown in a single line.

unused.quote: Let it come, as it will, and don’t / be afraid. God does not leave us / comfortless, so let evening come.
unused.source: Jane Kenyon, Let Evening Come, the final stanza, lines 16 to 18 (Graywolf Press, 1990)

unused.quote: We call it a grain of sand, / but it calls itself neither grain nor sand.
unused.source: Wisława Szymborska, View with a Grain of Sand, lines 1 to 2, Ludzie na moście (1986) (trans. Stanisław Barańczak and Clare Cavanagh, 1995)

unused.quote: Listen to the reed how it tells a tale, complaining of separations.
unused.source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, line 1 (trans. Reynold A. Nicholson, 1926)
unused.note: Verified opening line. Nicholson later revised it after the oldest manuscript to Listen to this reed how it complains; the 1926 wording ships with the 1926 date. Held for a quieter month.

unused.quote: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit.
unused.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Hobbit, ch. 1, ‘An Unexpected Party’, first sentence
unused.note: Verified opening line, pure delight; January had more openings than days. Mind the cap: the Calendar For Life bank carries many Tolkien lines.

unused.quote: Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.
unused.source: Simone Weil, letter to Joë Bousquet, 13 April 1942 (trans. Raymond Rosenthal, 1976, in Pétrement, Simone Weil: A Life, p. 462)
unused.note: Carried from January and held again: February took Weil’s What are you going through?, verified on the page, and one Weil per month. Page 462 rests on four scholarly citations. An attention line. Blocked by the cap: Simone Weil already stands three times in the year, in February, March and September, so this line cannot land at all. It should be retired rather than carried again.

unused.quote: I’ve learned to live simply, wisely, / To look at the sky and pray to God, / And to take long walks before evening / To wear out this useless anxiety.
unused.source: Anna Akhmatova, ‘I’ve learned to live simply, wisely’ (1912), Rosary (1914), lines 1 to 4 (trans. Judith Hemschemeyer, 1990)
unused.note: Verified on several independent reprints credited to Hemschemeyer, confidence medium: the Zephyr volume was not opened and no page is cited. Tidier source: Rosary (1914). A quiet daily practice: October.

unused.quote: Patience, patience, patience, is what the sea teaches. Patience and faith. One should lie empty, open, choiceless as a beach—waiting for a gift from the sea.
unused.source: Anne Morrow Lindbergh, Gift from the Sea, chapter 1, The Beach (Pantheon, 1955)
unused.note: Verified. It is a stillness line, not a road line.

unused.quote: When the spirit swells my breast I love to roam leisurely among the green hills; or sometimes, sitting on the brink of the murmuring Missouri, I marvel at the great blue overhead.
unused.source: Zitkala-Ša, The Great Spirit, American Indian Stories, opening sentence (Hayworth Publishing House, 1921)
unused.note: Verified. The refuter called its fit for April honest rather than exact: it is a marvelling line, so it goes to the month of stillness.

unused.quote: The time that my journey takes is long and the way of it long. I came out on the chariot of the first gleam of light, and pursued my voyage through the wildernesses of worlds leaving my track on many a star and planet.
unused.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (Song Offerings), poem 12, opening two paragraphs (trans. the author, 1912)
unused.note: Verified. The long journey inward, which suits the month of stillness better than the month of setting out.

unused.quote: One day as I was sitting alone in my study surrounded by books on all kinds of subjects, devoting myself to literary studies, my usual habit, my mind dwelt at length on the weighty opinions of various authors whom I had studied for a long time.
unused.source: Christine de Pizan, The Book of the City of Ladies, Part One, ch. 1, the opening sentence (trans. Earl Jeffrey Richards, 1982)
unused.note: Corrected: the whole opening sentence is restored from the Richards translation. Held: it sets a scene in a study, which suits the month of the quiet room.

unused.quote: Do nothing which is of no use.
unused.source: Miyamoto Musashi, A Book of Five Rings, the Ground Book, the last of the nine rules for learning the Way (trans. Victor Harris, 1974)
unused.note: Verified, medium confidence on the Harris translation. Held: do nothing which is of no use is a rule of attention.

unused.quote: Men may dyen of ymaginacioun, / So depe may impressioun be take.
unused.source: Geoffrey Chaucer, The Canterbury Tales, The Miller’s Tale, lines 3612 to 3613, The Riverside Chaucer (the Miller)
unused.note: Verified in the Riverside lineation. Middle English on the page, which suits a month with room for older spelling.

unused.quote: I hope it is no very cynical asperity not to confess obligations where no benefit has been received, or to be unwilling that the Publick should consider me as owing that to a Patron, which Providence has enabled me to do for myself.
unused.source: Samuel Johnson, letter to Lord Chesterfield, 7 February 1755, in Boswell, Life of Johnson, under 1755
unused.note: Corrected to the wording Boswell prints, with obligations in the plural and Publick in the old spelling. The manuscript behind the Hyde edition differs again.

unused.quote: I’ll make my report as if I told a story, for I was taught as a child on my homeworld that Truth is a matter of the imagination.
unused.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, The Left Hand of Darkness, chapter 1, opening sentence (Genly Ai)
unused.note: Verified as the first sentence of Genly Ai’s report. Truth as a matter of the imagination, which is a strong line for any month about story.

unused.quote: The writer should never be ashamed of staring. There is nothing that doesn’t require his attention.
unused.source: Flannery O’Connor, Mystery and Manners, The Nature and Aim of Fiction (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1969)
unused.note: Verified in Mystery and Manners. Attention as a discipline, which suits a month about looking.

unused.quote: I, too, dislike it.
unused.source: Marianne Moore, Poetry, line 1, Complete Poems (Macmillan and Viking, 1967)
unused.note: Corrected to the three line final text of 1967, because the printings of 1919 and 1924 read I too, dislike it with one comma.

unused.quote: The universe is made of stories, / not of atoms.
unused.source: Muriel Rukeyser, The Speed of Darkness, section IX (Random House, 1968)
unused.note: Verified in section IX of The Speed of Darkness. Stories rather than atoms, a line about what the world is made of.

unused.quote: We tell ourselves stories in order to live.
unused.source: Joan Didion, The White Album, the title essay, opening sentence (Simon and Schuster, 1979)
unused.note: Verified opening line. The essay goes on to test the claim, so the line is cooler than it reads alone; a truth-and-clarity line.

unused.quote: Man is least himself when he talks in his own person. Give him a mask, and he will tell you the truth.
unused.source: Oscar Wilde, The Critic as Artist, Part II, in Intentions, 1891 (Gilbert)
unused.note: Verified. Held: the mask line is about how truth gets said, so it wants the month of plain speech.

unused.quote: Do you not see how necessary a World of Pains and troubles is to school an Intelligence and make it a soul?
unused.source: John Keats, letter to George and Georgiana Keats, 14 February to 3 May 1819, the entry of 21 April (ed. Gittings, 1970)
unused.note: Verified. Held: the world of pains that schools an intelligence is a line about becoming, not about holding.

unused.quote: The unknown, the unforetold, the unproven, that is what life is based on. Ignorance is the ground of thought. Unproof is the ground of action.
unused.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, The Left Hand of Darkness, ch. 5, The Domestication of Hunch (Faxe) (1969)
unused.note: Corrected: the novel reads the unproven, not the unprovable. Held: ignorance as the ground of thought is a line about not knowing rather than about courage.

unused.quote: Nevertheless, not to extinguish our free will, I hold it to be true that Fortune is the arbiter of one-half of our actions, but that she still leaves us to direct the other half, or perhaps a little less.
unused.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, chapter XXV (trans. W. K. Marriott, 1908)
unused.note: Verified. Held: fortune and the half we still direct is a line about agency, and the Philosophy lane was full.

unused.quote: To conquer fear is the beginning of wisdom, in the pursuit of truth as in the endeavour after a worthy manner of life.
unused.source: Bertrand Russell, Unpopular Essays, ch. 7, An Outline of Intellectual Rubbish (George Allen and Unwin, 1950)
unused.note: Corrected: the spelling follows the George Allen and Unwin text, which reads endeavour. Held: to conquer fear is the beginning of wisdom sits close to Kant, and Kant took the day.

unused.quote: What is there / like fortitude! What sap / went through that little thread / to make the cherry red!
unused.source: Marianne Moore, Nevertheless, the last four lines, in the collection Nevertheless (Macmillan, 1944)
unused.note: Corrected: the quotation now starts at What is there, so the verse keeps Moore own line breaks. Held: the Poetry lane was the fattest in the month.

unused.quote: Tell me about a complicated man.
unused.source: Homer, The Odyssey, Book 1, line 1 (trans. Emily Wilson, 2017)
unused.note: Verified opening line of Wilson’s Odyssey. Held because January had more openings than days; a line for hard roads.

unused.quote: Yes, of course it hurts when buds are breaking. Why else would the springtime falter?
unused.source: Karin Boye, Yes, Of Course It Hurts, lines 1 and 2, För trädets skull (1935) (trans. David McDuff, 1994)
unused.note: Verified in McDuff. Held because April landed the other Boye, and one person may stand once a month; the pain of growth suits the month of courage.

unused.quote: Living is no laughing matter: / you must live with great seriousness / like a squirrel, for example— / I mean without looking for something beyond and above living, / I mean living must be your whole occupation.
unused.source: Nâzim Hikmet, On Living, Part I, opening lines, in Poems of Nazim Hikmet (trans. Randy Blasing and Mutlu Konuk, 1994)
unused.note: Verified. Held: living with great seriousness is a charge to hold on, which is July.

unused.quote: I wished to tell the truth, for truth always conveys its own moral to those who are able to receive it.
unused.source: Anne Brontë, The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, Preface to the Second Edition, 22 July 1848
unused.note: Verified in the Preface to the second edition of 1848. A plain statement of purpose.

unused.quote: You can’t get away from yourself by moving from one place to another.
unused.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, Book I, chapter 2 (Jake Barnes)
unused.note: Verified, Jake to Robert Cohn. It corrects the traveller rather than sending him out, so it reads as a truth line and not an April line.

unused.quote: Some races wax and others wane, and in a short space the tribes of living things are changed, and like runners hand on the torch of life.
unused.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura, Book II, lines 77 to 79 (trans. Cyril Bailey, 1910)

unused.quote: Duration is the continuous progress of the past which gnaws into the future and which swells as it advances.
unused.source: Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution, chapter I (trans. Arthur Mitchell, 1911)

unused.quote: Life is not a series of gig lamps symmetrically arranged; life is a luminous halo, a semi-transparent envelope surrounding us from the beginning of consciousness to the end.
unused.source: Virginia Woolf, Modern Fiction, The Common Reader (Hogarth Press, 1925)
unused.note: Corrected the wording. The Common Reader of 1925 reads life is a luminous halo. The reading but a luminous halo belongs to the earlier version of the essay, Modern Novels, printed in the Times Literary Supplement in 1919.

unused.quote: I think we are well advised to keep on nodding terms with the people we used to be, whether we find them attractive company or not.
unused.source: Joan Didion, Slouching Towards Bethlehem, On Keeping a Notebook (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1968)

unused.quote: The public must decide whether it wishes to continue on the present road, and it can do so only when in full possession of the facts.
unused.source: Rachel Carson, Silent Spring, chapter 2, The Obligation to Endure (Houghton Mifflin, 1962)
unused.note: Verified in chapter 2 of Silent Spring. Full possession of the facts, a public truth line.

unused.quote: I’m nobody! Who are you? / Are you nobody, too?
unused.source: Emily Dickinson, ‘I’m nobody! Who are you?’, Poems, Second Series, Life I, lines 1 to 2 (Roberts Brothers, 1891)
unused.note: Verified in Poems, Second Series of 1891. Two lines only, in that edition’s lineation.

unused.quote: Beauty is no quality in things themselves: It exists merely in the mind which contemplates them; and each mind perceives a different beauty.
unused.source: David Hume, Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary, Of the Standard of Taste (ed. Miller, pp. 229 to 230)
unused.note: Corrected in re-verification. Held: Hume sets the sentence out as the sceptical case and the next paragraph restrains it, so it wants a month about seeing clearly.

unused.quote: Music was my refuge. I could crawl into the spaces between the notes and curl my back to loneliness.
unused.source: Maya Angelou, Singin’ and Swingin’ and Gettin’ Merry Like Christmas, chapter 1, the opening sentences (Random House, 1976)
unused.note: Verified. Held: Maya Angelou stands in July with Still I Rise, and one person may stand once a month.

unused.quote: That’s no way to treat adventures. Never say ‘no’ to adventures. Always say ‘yes’, otherwise you’ll lead a very dull life.
unused.source: Ian Fleming, Chitty-Chitty-Bang-Bang: The Magical Car, Adventure Number Two (Commander Caractacus Pott) (Jonathan Cape, 1964)
unused.note: Verified. Held: Commander Pott’s counsel is about saying yes to danger, which suits a month of trial.

unused.quote: Travel is in my opinion a very profitable exercise; the soul is there continually employed in observing new and unknown things, and I do not know, as I have often said a better school wherein to model life than by incessantly exposing to it the diversity of so many other lives, fancies, and usances, and by making it relish a perpetual variety of forms of human nature.
unused.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book III, ch. 9, Of Vanity (trans. Charles Cotton, revised by W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)
unused.note: Verified. Another Montaigne is already held for May, so this goes on to the month of clear seeing. Blocked by the cap as of October: Montaigne now stands three times in the year, in May, June and October, so this second Montaigne line cannot land. It should be retired rather than carried again.

unused.quote: In Louisville, at the corner of Fourth and Walnut, in the center of the shopping district, I was suddenly overwhelmed with the realization that I loved all those people, that they were mine and I theirs, that we could not be alien to one another even though we were total strangers.
unused.source: Thomas Merton, Conjectures of a Guilty Bystander, Part Three, The Night Spirit and the Dawn Air (Doubleday, 1966)
unused.note: Corrected the tradition from Diary to Essay. Conjectures prints no dated entries. It is arranged in five titled parts, and the book describes itself as notes, opinions, experiences and reflections based on notebooks Merton kept since 1956. Part Three appeared as an essay in New Blackfriars in 1965. Merton’s dated journal is the separate A Search for Solitude.

unused.quote: Caring involves stepping out of one’s own personal frame of reference into the other’s.
unused.source: Nel Noddings, Caring: A Feminine Approach to Ethics and Moral Education, ch. 1, p. 24 (University of California Press, 1984)

unused.quote: Your silence will not protect you.
unused.source: Audre Lorde, Sister Outsider, The Transformation of Silence into Language and Action, p. 41 (The Crossing Press, 1984)
unused.note: Corrected: this is not new prose of 1984. Lorde delivered it as a paper at the Modern Language Association panel on lesbians and literature on 28 December 1977, and it was first printed in Sinister Wisdom in 1978. The wording and page given are those of Sister Outsider.

unused.quote: To sin by silence, when we should protest, / Makes cowards out of men. The human race / Has climbed on protest.
unused.source: Ella Wheeler Wilcox, Protest, lines 1 to 3, Poems of Problems, p. 154 (W. B. Conkey, 1914)

unused.quote: Good prose is like a window pane.
unused.source: George Orwell, Why I Write, the final paragraph (Gangrel, No. 4, Summer 1946)
unused.note: Verified in the final paragraph of Gangrel, Summer 1946. Held because Orwell can stand once in a month.

unused.quote: God offers to every mind its choice between truth and repose.
unused.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Intellect, essay XI in Essays: First Series (1841)
unused.note: Verified in essay XI of Essays: First Series. Truth or repose, and the choice is the whole line.

unused.quote: He that would seriously set upon the search of truth, ought in the first place to prepare his mind with a love of it.
unused.source: John Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book IV, ch. XIX, Of Enthusiasm, section 1 (ed. Fraser, 1894, vol. II, p. 428)
unused.note: Corrected against Fraser’s Clarendon edition of 1894, which keeps the comma after truth. Of Enthusiasm was added in the fourth edition of 1700.

unused.quote: Never did eye see the sun unless it had first become sunlike, and never can the soul have vision of the First Beauty unless itself be beautiful.
unused.source: Plotinus, Enneads, I.6.9, On Beauty (trans. Stephen MacKenna, 1917)
unused.note: Verified in MacKenna 1917. A clarity line rather than a beginning line.

unused.quote: For to be possessed of a vigorous mind is not enough; the prime requisite is rightly to apply it.
unused.source: René Descartes, Discourse on the Method, Part I, first paragraph (trans. John Veitch, 1850)
unused.note: Verified in Veitch; the 1850 date is from memory, not from a scan. Right application of the mind: a clarity line.

unused.quote: The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.
unused.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, proposition 5.6 (trans. C. K. Ogden, 1922)
unused.note: Verified. Held because Wittgenstein can appear once in a month and proposition 7 is the stronger line for a quieter month.

unused.quote: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
unused.source: Francis Bacon, Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Of Studies (1625)
unused.note: Verified. Held only because Bacon lands in May with Read not to contradict; one person a month.

unused.quote: All men by nature desire to know.
unused.source: Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book I, ch. 1, 980a21 (trans. W. D. Ross, 1908)
unused.note: Verified opening of the Metaphysics. Held: all men by nature desire to know is the appetite for truth.

unused.quote: The answer must be, I think, that beauty and grace are performed whether or not we will or sense them. The least we can do is try to be there.
unused.source: Annie Dillard, Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, chapter 1, Heaven and Earth in Jest (Harper’s Magazine Press, 1974)

unused.quote: I did not care what it was all about. All I wanted to know was how to live in it. Maybe if you found out how to live in it you learned from that what it was all about.
unused.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, Book II, chapter 14 (Jake Barnes) (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1926)
unused.note: Verified in the Scribner text of 1926. Held: Jake wants to know how to live in it, which is a search for clarity.

unused.quote: There is no foreign land; it is the traveller only that is foreign, and now and again, by a flash of recollection, lights up the contrasts of the earth.
unused.source: Robert Louis Stevenson, The Silverado Squatters, Part II, With the Children of Israel, chapter III, The Return (Chatto and Windus, 1883)
unused.note: Corrected: the sentence is in The Return, Part II. Held: it is the traveller only that is foreign is a correction of the eye, which is June.

report.thinnestLane: Correspondence: four proposed, three survived, all three used, none spare (Fiction ties at three survivors)
